title: Beyond compliance: why teachers need growth, not just professional development
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Reading C. M. Smith's study of 26 elementary teachers, Hughes draws out a contradiction schools rarely notice: teachers are required to differentiate, adapt and exercise judgement for pupils, while the development built for them is standardised and compliance-driven. Teachers in the study did not treat growth as a personal luxury but as an extension of their work with pupils; what they met instead was initiative fatigue, admin burden and training delivered by people long out of the classroom. Hughes's central objection is that CPD systems mistake efficiency for quality, treating a teacher of three years and a teacher of thirty as interchangeable and eroding professional trust in the process. The essay is strongest when it turns to leadership, distinguishing genuine instructional influence from symbolic roles that hand teachers responsibility without authority - what she bluntly calls additional labour dressed up as opportunity. It also names the false binary of career progression, where the only way to lead is to leave the classroom, and reports the study's alternatives: master teacher roles, hybrid teaching-coaching posts, curriculum specialists and protected collaboration time. Smith's transformational-leadership frame supplies the diagnosis that PD lacks individualised consideration and intellectual stimulation. Hughes's own conclusion refuses to separate retention from development and puts an uncomfortable question to leaders: does the professional culture actually assume that teachers think?
points: The double standard is the argument's hinge - systems that demand differentiation for children deliver undifferentiated training to adults.
Teachers asked for time to implement, revise, reflect and talk rather than better materials or better speakers, which reframes CPD quality as a scheduling problem.
Hughes separates informal leadership - mentoring, modelling, curriculum thinking - from formal roles, and argues its invisibility is what quietly wastes accumulated expertise.
The binary between staying in the classroom and leaving for management is treated as a structural flaw that strips expertise out of classrooms.
Her final claim is that empowerment is not a moral nicety but an instructional-quality mechanism: disempowerment reduces professional learning to technical compliance.
quotes: Teachers are expected to differentiate for pupils, respond to context, exercise judgement and adapt constantly. Yet the professional development designed for them is often standardised and compliance-driven.

Teachers enter the profession with expertise, commitment and intrinsic motivation, but many become disenchanted when their knowledge is undervalued and their opportunities for influence are restricted. Smith identifies a central contradiction: teachers are expected to personalise learning for children, while the professional learning they receive is frequently standardised and disconnected from classroom realities.
Too much CPD still assumes that efficiency is the same thing as quality. If everyone receives the same training, the thinking goes, the organisation is aligned.
Teachers in the study did not simply want better materials or more interesting speakers. They wanted time to implement, revise, reflect and talk.

Schools often congratulate themselves for “creating leadership opportunities” when what they have really created is additional labour. Smith shows that teachers were not rejecting leadership; they were rejecting hollow versions of it.
Teachers do not stay in schools because they are merely managed efficiently. They are more likely to stay when they can see themselves growing, contributing and being taken seriously.

If there is a challenge here for school leaders, it is not just to improve the quality of CPD sessions. It is to ask a more uncomfortable question: does our professional culture actually assume that teachers think?
